_warning: Prices, turnaround times and centering tolerances change CONSTANTLY, and in 2026 AVAILABILITY changes faster than either. Three of the five companies here have their cheapest tiers switched off right now (PSA Value paused 2026-06-02, BGS Base/Standard sold out 2026-08-05, TAG Basic/Standard/Express paused 2026-05-01 and 2026-05-28). Every tier therefore carries an 'available' flag — read it before you quote a price. Centering bands below remain a transparent approximation; the real algorithms (esp. BGS) are proprietary.
_availabilityWarning: READ THIS BEFORE TRUSTING A FEE. `cheapestTier()` in card-grader.html sorts fees[company] by price and returns [0] with NO availability check, so it still picks tiers this file marks available:false — the BGS Base row at $17.95 and the TAG Basic row at $22 are both unbuyable today and both are still the cheapest number in their arrays. Data alone cannot fix that; the sort needs a `.filter(t => t.available !== false)` and this file cannot supply one. Until that lands, the 'Should I grade it?' economics for BGS and TAG are computed on prices nobody can pay. The unavailable rows are kept rather than deleted on purpose: they are the record of what the tier costs when it reopens, and deleting them would hide the problem instead of naming it.

fx._note: Multiply AUD by audUsd to get USD. ECB daily reference fixing via Frankfurter, read 2026-08-23 (latest publication was 2026-08-21). This is a MID-MARKET rate: the owner banks AUD, and the card he actually pays PSA/BGS/CGC/TAG with will land 2-4% worse once the issuer's international fee and spread are applied. Nothing here adds that margin — a USD fee shown in this file is the sticker price, not the bank statement. Only PCG quotes in AUD; every other company's figures below are native USD and are NOT converted.

submissionCosts._note: AU -> US round trip, PER BATCH, not per card — and that is the whole point. The per-card model everywhere else in this tool cannot express a fixed cost that one card and thirty cards share, so a single card carries the entire ~$130 round trip while thirty carry ~$4.30 each. Read every per-card economics number in the report as excluding this block until the caller divides it by the batch size itself. shippingUsd 50 is an ESTIMATE: Australia Post Zone 3 (Americas) for a ~500g parcel, roughly AUD 40 Pack & Track / AUD 70 International Express under the rates effective 2026-07-01, converted at fx.audUsd — third-party rate table (hotsnail.com.au, read 2026-08-23), not verified against a live auspost.com.au quote for the owner's actual parcel. insurancePct 4 is Australia Post Extra Cover, AUD 4.00 per AUD 100 (or part thereof) of declared value on items AUD 100-5,000, i.e. 4% of declared value with an AUD 5,000 ceiling — above that the outbound leg cannot be fully covered at any price. returnShippingUsd 79.99 is SOURCED and exact: PSA's published international return chart, 10-19 items at the $15,000 max-insured band (psacard.com/info/postage, read 2026-08-23; 1-4 items is $69.99, 50+ adds $1.49/item). It is used as the stand-in for all five companies because only PSA publishes a chart — BGS, CGC, TAG and PCG return shipping is unverified here. NOT included and NOT estimated: US import duty. The USD 800 de minimis exemption has been suspended since 2025-08-29 and from 2026-07-24 CBP charges per 10-digit HS code and country of origin, so the inbound leg now attracts duty that depends on the cards themselves. PCG is the exception to this entire block — it is a domestic AU submission with no international leg at all, which is a real part of its value that its marketFactor discount has to be weighed against.

psa10VsPsa9Note: For modern Pokemon, PSA 10 typically sells for 2-5x a PSA 9 — the '9-vs-10 cliff' is where the value and the prediction error both live.

PSA.label: PSA
PSA.known: Deepest resale liquidity; the de-facto market reference.
PSA._marketFactorNote: 1.0 BY DEFINITION — PSA is the reference every other marketFactor is measured against, not a measured value. It is the right reference because it is where the comps are: GemRate via Yahoo Sports put PSA at 72% of 2025 graded volume (76% sports, 69% TCG), which is why a PSA comp exists for almost any card and the other four often have none.

BGS.label: BGS (Beckett)
BGS.known: Mandatory 4 subgrades on every slab; coveted Black Label (all four 10s). The famous trio is Black 10 / Gold 10 / Gem Mint 9.5 — two 10s exist, and the 9.5 shares the gold label.
BGS._marketFactorNote: ESTIMATE, and the one number in this block that is most wrong at the extremes — a single scalar genuinely cannot describe BGS. At the top BGS beats PSA outright: one 2026 dataset of ~57,190 Pokemon cards put the median BGS 10 multiplier at 31.9x raw versus PSA's 24.5x, and Black Label 10s are reported selling at 1.5-3x the PSA 10 price (fewer than ~0.1% of submissions earn one). At 9 and below the same slab trades under the equivalent PSA grade, because the subgrades printed on the label give a buyer reasons to pay less that a bare PSA 9 never surfaces. 0.95 is a deliberate blend that is too low for a Pristine 10 and too high for a BGS 8; treat it as a placeholder for a grade-dependent curve nobody here has fitted. Sources: pokemonpricetracker.com and phantomdisplay.com resale comparisons, read 2026-08-23 — hobby analysis, not exchange data.
BGS._tenTiersNote: Beckett's OWN words (beckett.com/grading + their 'Walking Through the BGS Process' article, read 2026-08-22): Black Label = all four subgrades 10; the ONLY difference for a gold-label Pristine 10 is ONE 9.5 among THREE 10s; Gem Mint 9.5 needs three 9.5s with the fourth no lower than 9. gradeGates enforce those combinations — a weighted average alone would award 10s Beckett's rules refuse. Re-read 2026-08-23: beckett.com/grading now states the label split as Black for perfect Pristine 10s, Gold for Pristine 10 and Gem Mint 9.5, Silver for everything else — consistent with the gates above, so they are unchanged.

CGC.label: CGC
CGC.known: Price/speed/consistency; subgrades discontinued on new slabs. Two 10s: Gem Mint 10, and Pristine 10 above it (special label). As of 2026-08-23 the only one of the five with NOTHING paused — every tier is orderable.
CGC._marketFactorNote: ESTIMATE from a wide and genuinely disputed spread. Narrow readings put modern CGC 10s within 5-10% of PSA 10 (a Mega Lucario ex SIR at ~$1,078 PSA vs ~$980 CGC, ~9%; a CGC Pristine 10 Mega Zygarde ex SIR reportedly outsold its PSA equivalent), wider readings put CGC 10s at 75-85% of PSA. Vintage is worse for CGC than modern, consistently reported at a 15-20% PSA premium. 0.85 sits mid-spread and leans to the pessimistic side because the store's mix is not all-modern. Sources: misprint.com, polkastarter.com, pokemonpricetracker.com comparisons, read 2026-08-23 — hobby analysis, not exchange data. One real complication the number hides: CGC's two 10s are not the same product, and a Pristine 10 does not trade like a Gem Mint 10.
CGC._tenTiersNote: CGC's published scale (cgccards.com/card-grading/grading-scale, read 2026-08-22): Pristine 10 = virtually flawless, centering 50/50; Gem Mint 10 = a 10 where one criterion falls short, centering not to exceed ~55/45 front / 75/25 back. Pristine's back tolerance is unpublished — 60 is a conservative approximation. No current subgrade mechanism is published (subgrades discontinued), so the tiers here key on centering alone.

PCG.label: PCG (Premier)
PCG.known: AU-market local grader (NZ-registered; drop-off Good Games Parramatta). Publishes numeric centering bands. Three 10s: Gem Mint -> Pristine -> Flawless (quad-10, gold label). Resale: AU market discounts PCG slabs vs the same PSA grade (~0.4-0.7x, estimate) and they sell slower. The offsetting advantage no other company here has: it is a domestic submission, so none of submissionCosts applies.
PCG._marketFactorNote: ESTIMATE, and the weakest-evidenced number in this file — SAY SO when it is quoted. No PCG price ladder exists anywhere and no dataset of PCG-vs-PSA same-grade sales was found in the 2026-08-23 research pass; searching for one returned only the general observation that non-incumbent slabs sell at a discount and that a locally graded AU slab is recognised less internationally than a PSA or BGS one. 0.55 is simply the midpoint of the ~0.4-0.7x range this config's own prose has carried since 2026-06-24, which was itself an owner-side estimate. It is a placeholder for a measurement, not a measurement. The honest way to improve it is the store's own eBay AU sold data once enough PCG slabs have moved through it.
PCG._tenTiersNote: PUBLISHED (grading-standards page, read 2026-08-22): Flawless = 50/50 both axes front AND back + no visible defects on any subgrade (quad 10; gold metal label); Pristine = 50/50 front, 60/40-or-better back; Gem Mint = 55/45 front, 60/40 back. 51 encodes 'measures 50/50' — a real card never measures exactly 50.000, and the config already encodes BGS's 50/50 the same way.

TAG.label: TAG
TAG.known: AI/computer-vision grading; richest digital report (DIG). Deeply capacity-constrained through 2026 — every tier under $149 has been shut since May.
TAG._marketFactorNote: ESTIMATE, but the best-sourced of the non-PSA four: multiple 2026 reviews independently report TAG slabs selling 35-60% below the equivalent PSA grade (narrower on modern, wider on vintage where PSA's brand is strongest), i.e. a 0.40-0.65 factor. 0.5 is the midpoint. Sources: tcgtreasury.com, misprint.com, read 2026-08-23 — hobby analysis, not exchange data. Worth stating alongside the number rather than hiding behind it: TAG's own pitch is grading accuracy and a documented report, not liquidity, so a 0.5 factor is the expected cost of that choice and not evidence the grade is wrong.

centering._doc: Per grade, 'front' and 'back' are the MAX allowed larger-side percentage on the worst axis (e.g. 55 means up to 55/45). A measured larger-side % must be <= the band to qualify for that grade. Bands ordered best to worst. Omit 'back' to leave the back unconstrained (SGC).
centering._bgsNote: Band-10 back tightened 60->55 per beckett.com/grading (the newer of Beckett's two live scale pages; the legacy /grading/scale page still says 60/40), read 2026-08-22. RE-VERIFIED 2026-08-23 on beckett.com/grading, which states Pristine 10 centering as '50/50 all around on front. 55/45 or better on back.' — the 51/55 pair below is that sentence encoded, and the tighter number stands. The published Pristine criteria are IDENTICAL for both 10s — the black/gold split is purely the subgrade combination (companies.BGS.gradeGates).
centering._pcgNote: PCG PUBLISHES these bands (premiercardgrading.com.au/pages/grading-standards, read 2026-08-22) — the one company here whose numbers are not approximations. This band list answers 'what earns A 10' (Gem Mint's 55/60); WHICH 10 — Gem Mint / Pristine / Flawless — is the tenTiers list on the company entry, applied as a label refinement from the measured centering + subgrades. 10/9 share 55/60 on a worst-axis model, so the 9 band is documentation, not logic; same for 7.5 vs 8.
centering._centeringRefreshNote: The 2026-08-23 refresh pass was a FEES and AVAILABILITY refresh. Only the BGS band-10 pair was re-checked against a live page; the PSA, CGC, PCG and TAG band tables below are carried forward from 2026-06-24 / 2026-08-22 unverified this pass. They are tolerances, not prices, and they move far more slowly than fees — but 'did not move' is an assumption here, not a re-read.

fees._doc: Base grading fee in USD per card and on-site turnaround in BUSINESS days (excludes shipping transit). All five companies publish in business days or explicitly define their unit as such, so nothing here is converted from calendar days — see _unitsNote. maxValueUsd = the tier's declared-value / insurance cap. available = orderable on 2026-08-23; note explains every false. minCards = the tier's minimum submission size. turnaroundDaysRange = the official published range where a range is published, with turnaroundDays as its midpoint so single-number consumers stay honest. turnaroundDaysObserved = what submitters are actually reporting, present ONLY where a sourced figure exists.
fees._unitsNote: Unit normalisation, checked per company rather than assumed. PSA publishes 'Business Days' on the tier cards. BGS publishes 'business days' per service level. CGC publishes 'working days' and its own FAQ defines them as Monday-Friday excluding public holidays, i.e. business days — the two words are the same unit at CGC. TAG's pricing footnote states estimates 'are measured in business days and exclude weekends, holidays, and carrier transit time'. PCG publishes BOTH forms and supplies its own conversion ('2 to 4 Weeks (10-20 Business Days)' = 5 business days per week); its Standard Bulk '6 to 8 Weeks' carries no gloss, so 30-40 business days below applies PCG's own stated rate to PCG's own stated weeks. NONE of these include transit — an AU submitter adds roughly 1-2 weeks each way on top of every number in this file.
fees._observedNote: turnaroundDaysObserved appears exactly once, on PSA Regular, because it is the only per-tier observed figure this pass could source. The rest is stated rather than guessed: BGS, CGC and PCG published no observed data and none was found, so those tiers carry no observed field at all. TAG is the interesting gap — TAG itself confirms slippage in plain language on its backlog tracker ('many orders are running past their estimated completion date', backlog at 134% of monthly processing capacity, down from a 420% peak) but publishes no per-tier day count, so inventing one would be fabricating precision TAG declined to give.

PSA.note: Cheapest PSA tier that can be bought — the four Value tiers ($24.99 Value Bulk through $64.99 Value Max) have been paused to new submissions since 2026-06-02 and are deliberately not listed here (see _psaNote). PSA._observedNote: 55 is a THIRD-PARTY tracker figure (cardgrader.ai, article dated 2026-08-15, reporting 50-60 days; pregradecards.com reports 40-60 over the same window) and it is BELOW PSA's own 70-80 estimate — the opposite of the usual direction, because PSA re-baselined the official number upward during the backlog. Two caveats worth carrying: the trackers do not state whether their days are business or calendar, and a figure that flatters the vendor deserves more suspicion than one that does not. disclaimers: Estimate only — this is NOT an official grade or a guarantee. Grading companies make the final call and outcomes vary on resubmission.

Surface and the card back are systematically under-assessed from photos. Fine scratches, print/roller lines and creases may not be visible. Inspect under bright directional (raking) light at multiple tilt angles.
No authentication. This tool predicts grade, not genuineness. High-value cards (e.g. Charizard secret rares) are heavily counterfeited — authenticate in hand.
Lower confidence on holo / refractor / gold / chrome surfaces, and at the 9-vs-10 boundary where most of the value (and the error) lives.
Centering is measured geometrically and is the most reliable signal; corners/edges/surface come from an AI vision pass and are advisory.
All prices and grading fees are point-in-time and change frequently.

PCG value-at-grade borrows PSA-slab prices (no PCG price ladder exists anywhere) — AU-market PCG slabs typically realise a substantial discount (~0.4-0.7x, estimate) vs the same PSA grade and sell slower. Treat PCG expected values as optimistic.

A cheap tier you cannot buy is not a cheap tier. As of 2026-08-23 PSA's four Value tiers, Beckett's Base and Standard, and TAG's Basic, Standard and Express are all closed to new submissions — check the 'available' flag on a tier before quoting its fee.
Quoted turnarounds are on-site business days and EXCLUDE transit. An Australian submission adds roughly 1-2 weeks each way on top, and every company states its estimate is not a guarantee.

Shipping, insurance and return postage are a per-BATCH cost (see submissionCosts) that the per-card economics on this page does not include. One card carries the whole round trip; thirty cards share it.

marketFactor is an ESTIMATE of what a company's slab realises against the same grade from PSA, drawn from published hobby analysis rather than exchange data — and for BGS a single number is actively misleading, because Black Label 10s command a large premium while lower BGS grades trade at a discount.
